conflicts.name: The Anglo-Spanish War and the Armada
conflicts.region: English Channel, Atlantic, Caribbean, Low Countries and Ireland
conflicts.religionRoleNote: Contemporaries on both sides understood the war as a struggle between Catholic and Protestant Christendom: Pius V had excommunicated and 'deposed' Elizabeth I in Regnans in Excelsis (1570), Philip II saw the 'Enterprise of England' as a service to God and the Church, and Sixtus V promised a million ducats once Spanish troops landed. Yet historians such as Garrett Mattingly, R. B. Wernham and Geoffrey Parker stress that strategy and commerce weighed as heavily: English aid to the Dutch rebels, English privateering against Spanish treasure fleets, the Portuguese succession and the security of the Spanish Netherlands. Parker's work on Philip II's 'messianic imperialism' argues that the king genuinely believed God would supply what his planning lacked, which makes religion more than a pretext; English Protestant identity, in turn, was hardened by the war. Religion is therefore best described as a major cause entangled with dynastic and economic rivalry.

leaders: Charles Howard, Lord Howard of Effingham

conflicts.summary: An undeclared but bitter war between Elizabethan England and Philip II's Spain, fought at sea, in the Netherlands, in the Caribbean and in Ireland. Its most famous episode, the failed 'Invincible Armada' of 1588, was blessed in Spain as a crusade to restore Catholicism in England and celebrated in England as a 'Protestant wind' sent by God. The war ended in stalemate with the Treaty of London in 1604.
conflicts.story:
Relations between England and Spain decayed steadily after Elizabeth I restored a Protestant church settlement in 1559. Pius V's bull Regnans in Excelsis (1570) declared the queen a heretic and released her subjects from obedience, which turned English Catholics into potential traitors in the eyes of the government. A series of plots to place the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots on the throne (Ridolfi 1571, Throckmorton 1583, Babington 1586) involved Spanish diplomats, while missionary priests trained at Douai and Rome entered England and were hunted and executed, among them the Jesuit Edmund Campion in 1581. At the same time English seamen such as John Hawkins and Francis Drake raided Spanish shipping and colonies, and Elizabeth's government quietly helped the Dutch Protestants in revolt against Philip II.

Open war followed the assassination of William of Orange in 1584 and Spain's alliance with the French Catholic League (Treaty of Joinville). In August 1585 Elizabeth signed the Treaty of Nonsuch, sending an army under the Earl of Leicester to the Netherlands; Philip had already seized English ships in Spanish ports. Drake sailed for the Caribbean and sacked Santo Domingo and Cartagena in 1586. The execution of Mary, Queen of Scots at Fotheringhay in February 1587 removed the Catholic claimant and made Philip, himself a descendant of Edward III, the obvious Catholic candidate. Drake's raid on Cádiz in April 1587, which destroyed stores and ships, delayed the planned invasion by a year.

The Armada of about 130 ships, commanded by the Duke of Medina Sidonia, left Lisbon in May 1588, sheltered at Corunna from storms and entered the Channel at the end of July. Its task was to escort the Duke of Parma's army of the Netherlands across from Flanders. A running fight past Plymouth, Portland and the Isle of Wight did little damage to either fleet, but the Spanish anchored off Calais without having made contact with Parma, whose barges were blockaded by Dutch flyboats. On the night of 7–8 August (new style) English fireships scattered the anchored fleet, and in the battle off Gravelines the next day the English inflicted serious damage. A south-westerly wind drove the Armada into the North Sea, and it returned to Spain by sailing around Scotland and the west of Ireland.

The return voyage became a catastrophe. Autumn gales wrecked perhaps two dozen ships on the Irish coast, at Streedagh Strand, Blasket Sound and elsewhere, and many survivors who reached land were killed by English garrisons or by order of the Lord Deputy, although some were sheltered by Irish lords. Perhaps a third of the ships never returned and the majority of deaths came from shipwreck, hunger and disease. English losses in battle were light, but typhus and dysentery killed thousands of English sailors in the weeks after the fighting, and Lord Howard complained bitterly that they were left unpaid and unfed.

The war did not end in 1588. An English 'Counter-Armada' under Drake and Sir John Norris in 1589 failed to take Lisbon or provoke a Portuguese rising and lost thousands of men. Spain rebuilt its navy and convoy system, and further armadas in 1596 and 1597 were dispersed by storms. Essex and Howard sacked Cádiz in 1596, while Drake and Hawkins died on an unsuccessful Caribbean expedition in 1595–96. Spain intervened in France on the side of the Catholic League and in Ireland on the side of Hugh O'Neill's rebellion (the Nine Years' War); a Spanish force landed at Kinsale in 1601 but the Irish and Spanish were defeated there in December 1601.

Philip II died in 1598 and Elizabeth in 1603. Her successor James VI and I, who wished to be a peacemaker, concluded the Treaty of London in August 1604. Neither side gained its principal aims: England remained Protestant, and Spain retained the southern Netherlands and its American trade. The treaty did not secure toleration for English Catholics, and the Gunpowder Plot of the following year showed how far confessional tension persisted.

In memory the Armada became central to English and later British Protestant identity. Medals, sermons and annual thanksgivings presented the defeat as a providential judgement in favour of the reformed religion, and the story was retold for centuries alongside John Foxe's Book of Martyrs. In Spain, theologians and preachers interpreted the disaster as a chastisement for the nation's sins rather than proof that the cause was wrong.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Philip II called the invasion 'the Enterprise of England' and regarded it as a work for God. The Armada's sailors confessed and received communion before sailing, swearing and gambling were forbidden on board, and the flagship's standard showed the crucified Christ with the Virgin and the words of Psalm 74 (73), 'Exsurge Domine et vindica causam tuam' ('Arise, O Lord, and judge thy cause'). Sixtus V renewed the excommunication of Elizabeth and promised a large subsidy once Spain landed, and Cardinal William Allen prepared an 'Admonition to the Nobility and People of England' calling Catholics to rise against a 'heretic' and 'usurper'. In England the government ordered prayers and fasts, and after the victory struck medals inscribed 'Flavit Jehovah et dissipati sunt' ('God blew and they were scattered'). A thanksgiving service was held at St Paul's in November 1588, and the 'Protestant wind' entered national mythology.
religiousCauses: Pius V's excommunication of Elizabeth I in 1570 declared her deposed and set loyalty to the pope against loyalty to the Crown.
Philip II saw himself as defender of Catholic Christendom and believed God required him to restore the Catholic faith in England.
English support for the Dutch Calvinist rebels was presented in England as solidarity with persecuted fellow Protestants.
The persecution and execution of Catholic priests and recusants in England was publicised in Spain and Rome as martyrdom requiring intervention.
The execution of the Catholic Mary, Queen of Scots in 1587 removed the Catholic heir and was portrayed as the killing of a martyr queen.
otherCauses: English privateering against Spanish treasure fleets and colonies threatened the finances on which Spanish power depended.
The Dutch Revolt made the security of the Spanish Netherlands and control of the Channel a vital strategic question.
Philip II's acquisition of Portugal in 1580 and his rivalry with France altered the balance of power in western Europe.
Commercial competition over Atlantic and Caribbean trade, including Hawkins's illegal slave-trading voyages, provoked repeated clashes.
Dynastic claims: Philip, descended from Edward III, saw himself as a candidate for the English crown after Mary Stuart's death.
triggers: The Treaty of Nonsuch (August 1585) committed English troops under Leicester to the Dutch rebels.
Philip II's seizure of English ships in Spanish harbours in May 1585.
Drake's West Indies raid of 1585–86 on Santo Domingo and Cartagena.
The execution of Mary, Queen of Scots at Fotheringhay on 8 February 1587.

timeline.text: Pius V issues Regnans in Excelsis, excommunicating Elizabeth I.
The Jesuit Edmund Campion is executed at Tyburn; harsher laws against recusants follow.
William of Orange is assassinated; Spain allies with the French Catholic League at Joinville.
Treaty of Nonsuch; open war begins and Drake sails for the Caribbean.
Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots; Drake raids Cádiz.
The Armada sails from Lisbon, is scattered by fireships off Calais and defeated at Gravelines; many ships are wrecked off Ireland.
The English Counter-Armada under Drake and Norris fails at Corunna and Lisbon.
Anglo-Dutch sack of Cádiz; a second Spanish armada is broken by storms.
A third Spanish armada is dispersed by gales in the Bay of Biscay.
A Spanish force lands at Kinsale to support Hugh O'Neill but is defeated in December.
The Treaty of London ends the war under James I and Philip III.

keyPeople.name: Elizabeth I
keyPeople.focus: Hesitant to fight an open war, she supported the Dutch rebels and privateers, approved the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots and rallied her forces at Tilbury in 1588.
keyPeople.outcome: Died in 1603 with the war unresolved; the Armada victory became the centrepiece of her legend as a Protestant queen.

keyPeople.name: Philip II of Spain
keyPeople.focus: Planned the Enterprise of England in close detail from the Escorial, convinced that God would favour a war waged for the Catholic faith.
keyPeople.outcome: Accepted the defeat as God's will, rebuilt his navy and sent further armadas; died in 1598.

keyPeople.name: Sir Francis Drake
keyPeople.focus: Raided the Caribbean in 1585–86, attacked Cádiz in 1587, served as vice-admiral against the Armada and led the failed Counter-Armada of 1589.
keyPeople.outcome: Died of dysentery off Portobelo in 1596 during an unsuccessful expedition; remembered as a hero in England and a pirate in Spain.

keyPeople.name: Alonso Pérez de Guzmán, Duke of Medina Sidonia
keyPeople.focus: Reluctantly took command after the death of the Marquis of Santa Cruz and kept the fleet in disciplined formation through the Channel.
keyPeople.outcome: Brought the surviving ships home and was blamed for the disaster, though modern historians judge him more fairly.

keyPeople.name: Alexander Farnese, Duke of Parma
keyPeople.focus: Assembled the invasion army and barges in Flanders but could not bring them out past the Dutch blockade to meet the Armada.
keyPeople.outcome: Diverted to campaigns in France against Henri IV; died of wounds in 1592.

keyPeople.name: Charles Howard, Lord Howard of Effingham
keyPeople.focus: Commanded the English fleet in 1588, ordered the fireship attack and later shared command of the 1596 raid on Cádiz.
keyPeople.outcome: Created Earl of Nottingham; later helped negotiate peace with Spain.

keyPeople.name: Cardinal William Allen
keyPeople.focus: Founded the English College at Douai and backed the invasion, preparing a printed admonition to English Catholics to rise in support of Spain.
keyPeople.outcome: The admonition was suppressed after the defeat; he died in Rome in 1594.

keyPeople.name: Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone
keyPeople.role: Leader of the Irish confederacy in the Nine Years' War
keyPeople.focus: Allied with Spain and presented his rebellion partly as a defence of the Catholic faith; his Spanish allies landed at Kinsale in 1601.
keyPeople.outcome: Defeated at Kinsale, submitted in 1603 and fled to the Continent in the Flight of the Earls (1607); died in Rome.

casualties.note: No reliable estimate exists for the deaths of the whole war, which was fought intermittently across several oceans and theatres. For the Armada campaign alone, Colin Martin and Geoffrey Parker and other historians suggest that well over 10,000 and perhaps up to 20,000 Spanish and Portuguese men died, mostly from shipwreck, disease, hunger and executions in Ireland rather than in battle; several thousand English sailors died of disease after the fighting. The 1589 Counter-Armada also lost thousands of men, mainly to sickness.

effects: England survived as an independent Protestant kingdom, and the threat of a Catholic restoration by foreign invasion receded.
Spain reformed its navy and convoy system, and its Atlantic treasure fleets continued largely unbroken; the war was a strategic stalemate rather than a turning point in Spanish power.
The Dutch Republic gained breathing space to consolidate its independence while Spain's resources were divided.
The war drew Ireland into continental confessional politics, linking Irish Catholic resistance to Spain and leading to the English conquest of Ulster after 1603.
The Treaty of London (1604) opened a period of Anglo-Spanish peace under James I but secured no toleration for English Catholics.
effectsOnChurch: English Catholics were increasingly portrayed as a potential fifth column, and penal laws against recusants and seminary priests were enforced with greater severity.
The 'Protestant wind' became a lasting part of English Protestant self-understanding as a providentially protected nation.
Disputes among English Catholic clergy over political involvement led to the Appellant controversy and declarations of loyalty to the Crown.
In Spain the defeat was interpreted in sermons as a divine chastisement, prompting calls for repentance rather than doubt about the cause.
conflicts.legacy: The Armada is one of the defining episodes of English national memory, often told as a Protestant David defeating a Catholic Goliath. Modern scholarship has complicated that story by stressing the role of weather, logistics and Parma's blockaded army, by recovering the war's Irish and Caribbean dimensions, and by showing that Spain remained a great power for decades afterwards. The war's mixture of genuine confessional conviction and hard strategic interest makes it a classic case of how religious and political motives reinforced one another in early modern Europe.

dissenters.name: Robert Southwell
dissenters.text: The Jesuit poet, later executed in 1595, wrote An Humble Supplication to Her Majesty (1591) protesting that English Catholics were loyal subjects who had no wish to see a foreign invasion, and pleading for an end to their persecution.

dissenters.name: Anthony Browne, Viscount Montague
dissenters.text: A Catholic peer who had opposed the anti-papal legislation in Parliament, he nonetheless rallied armed men for the queen in 1588, embodying the many English Catholics who refused to treat religion as a reason for treason.

dissenters.name: The Appellant priests
dissenters.text: In 1603 thirteen secular priests signed a Protestation of Allegiance to Elizabeth, repudiating papal claims to depose the monarch and Jesuit-backed plans for invasion as incompatible with Christian duty.

theatres.name: Cartagena de Indias, sacked by Drake
Cádiz raid ('singeing the King of Spain's beard')

campaigns.title: The voyage of the Spanish Armada
campaigns.people: Duke of Medina Sidonia and about 130 ships
campaigns.text: The Armada sailed from Lisbon in May, refitted at Corunna and fought a running battle up the Channel before anchoring off Calais. After the fireship attack and the battle of Gravelines it was driven into the North Sea and returned by the long route around Scotland and the west of Ireland, where gales wrecked many ships.

campaigns.title: Drake's West Indies raid
campaigns.people: Sir Francis Drake and Christopher Carleill
campaigns.text: A large privately financed expedition with royal backing raided the Galician coast, the Cape Verde islands and the heart of Spain's Caribbean empire, then evacuated the struggling English colonists from Roanoke on its way home. It brought little profit but damaged Spanish credit and prestige.

conflicts.name: The Thirty Years' War
conflicts.region: Holy Roman Empire (Germany, Bohemia, Austria) and neighbouring states
conflicts.religionRoleNote: The war began as a revolt of largely Protestant Bohemian estates against a Catholic Habsburg king and was fought along confessional lines for much of its first decade, culminating in the Edict of Restitution (1629). Older accounts therefore called it the last great war of religion that 'degenerated' into a political struggle once Catholic France allied with Lutheran Sweden against the Catholic Habsburgs. Peter H. Wilson argues that it was not primarily a religious war but a conflict over the constitutional order of the Empire and the European balance of power, in which confessional belief shaped how participants saw their aims; Lutheran Saxony fought for the emperor for long periods, and Catholic France subsidised Protestant armies. Other historians, such as Geoffrey Parker, also stress fiscal strain, the climate crisis of the 'Little Ice Age' and dynastic ambition. Religion was a major cause and an indispensable framework of meaning, but never the only one.

leaders: Philip IV of Spain and the Count-Duke of Olivares

conflicts.summary: A series of interlocking wars fought mainly in the Holy Roman Empire, beginning with the Bohemian revolt of 1618 and ending with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. Catholic and Protestant rulers invoked God throughout, and the struggle over the Edict of Restitution and the fate of Protestantism in Germany was real, but dynastic, constitutional and great-power interests increasingly dominated. The war devastated central Europe, killing perhaps a fifth of the Empire's population.
conflicts.story:
The Peace of Augsburg (1555) had allowed Lutheran and Catholic princes of the Empire to determine the religion of their territories, but it excluded Calvinists and left the fate of church lands unresolved. In the following decades confessional rivalry hardened: the Catholic duke of Bavaria occupied the Lutheran city of Donauwörth in 1607, Protestant princes formed the Union in 1608 and Catholics the League in 1609. In Bohemia, where Utraquists, Lutherans, Calvinists and the Unity of Brethren together outnumbered Catholics, the estates had wrung a Letter of Majesty guaranteeing religious freedom from Emperor Rudolf II in 1609. The election of the devout Catholic Ferdinand of Styria as king of Bohemia in 1617 alarmed them.

On 23 May 1618 Protestant nobles threw two royal governors and a secretary from a window of Prague Castle; all three survived, which Catholics attributed to the Virgin's intervention. The Bohemian estates raised an army, deposed Ferdinand in 1619 (just as he was elected emperor) and chose the Calvinist Elector Palatine Frederick V as their king. Frederick received little help from his Protestant allies, and on 8 November 1620 the army of the Catholic League under Tilly, with imperial troops, routed the Bohemians at the White Mountain outside Prague. Twenty-seven leaders of the revolt were executed in Prague's Old Town Square in June 1621, Protestant clergy were expelled, and over the following years Bohemia was forcibly re-Catholicised; thousands of Protestant families, including the Brethren bishop Jan Amos Comenius, went into exile. The Palatinate was conquered, and its famous library at Heidelberg was carried to Rome.

The war spread north. Christian IV of Denmark intervened as a Lutheran prince of the Empire and was defeated by Tilly at Lutter in 1626, while the imperial generalissimo Wallenstein built a vast army financed by contributions extorted from occupied lands. At the height of Catholic success Ferdinand II issued the Edict of Restitution (March 1629), ordering the return of all church lands secularised since 1552 and allowing Catholic rulers to expel Protestants. Encouraged by his Jesuit confessor Wilhelm Lamormaini, the emperor saw it as an act of justice before God; Protestants saw it as an existential threat, and even Catholic princes feared the emperor's growing power.

In July 1630 Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden landed in Pomerania, presenting himself as the protector of German Protestants while pursuing Swedish security in the Baltic, and in January 1631 he accepted subsidies from Catholic France in the Treaty of Bärwalde. On 20 May 1631 Tilly's troops stormed the Protestant city of Magdeburg; in the sack and the fire that followed some 20,000 of its perhaps 25,000 inhabitants died, and 'Magdeburgisation' became a byword for atrocity. Gustavus defeated Tilly at Breitenfeld in September 1631, swept through Catholic Franconia and the Rhineland into Bavaria, and was killed in his victory at Lützen in November 1632. Wallenstein, suspected of treasonable negotiations, was assassinated by his own officers at Eger in 1634. After the Swedish defeat at Nördlingen in 1634, the Peace of Prague (1635) suspended the Edict of Restitution and reconciled most Lutheran princes with the emperor.

The war did not end, because France now declared war on Spain (1635) and Sweden fought on. The final phase pitted Catholic France and Lutheran Sweden against the Catholic Habsburgs, with armies living off a ravaged countryside. Soldiers, camp followers and civilians died in their millions from plague, typhus, famine and violence; regions such as Pomerania, Mecklenburg, Württemberg and parts of Thuringia lost a third to a half of their people, while others were relatively spared. Atrocities were committed by every army, Protestant as well as Catholic, and the torture of peasants to reveal hidden goods became a stock image of the age.

Peace negotiations opened in the Westphalian towns of Münster (Catholic powers) and Osnabrück (Protestant powers) in 1643–44 and concluded with the treaties signed on 24 October 1648; Spain and the Dutch Republic had made a separate peace at Münster earlier that year. The Peace of Westphalia recognised Calvinism alongside Lutheranism and Catholicism, fixed 1 January 1624 as the 'normative year' for the possession of church property and public worship, protected private worship for religious minorities, and required that religious questions in the imperial diet be settled by agreement between Catholic and Protestant bodies rather than by majority vote. Sweden and France gained territory; the independence of the Dutch Republic and the Swiss Confederation was formally recognised.

Pope Innocent X protested in the brief Zelo domus Dei (dated November 1648) that the treaties harmed the Catholic Church, but the protest was ignored by Catholic as well as Protestant signatories. Westphalia is often described as the end of Europe's wars of religion and the beginning of a system of sovereign states. Historians now regard that as an exaggeration, but it did mark the point at which the major powers stopped trying to settle the religious division of Christendom by force within the Empire.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Both sides fought with chaplains, field sermons, prayers and hymns. Catholics attributed the victory at the White Mountain to the Virgin Mary; the Discalced Carmelite Dominic of Jesus and Mary accompanied the army with an image of the Nativity damaged by Calvinists, and the church of Santa Maria della Vittoria in Rome commemorated the triumph. Ferdinand II, educated by Jesuits, held that he must answer to God for the faith of his subjects, and his confessor Lamormaini urged the Edict of Restitution as a divine duty. Maximilian of Bavaria dedicated his realm to the Virgin and erected the Mariensäule in Munich in 1638. Gustavus Adolphus imposed daily prayer on his army, which used 'Gott mit uns' as a field word at Breitenfeld, and Protestant pamphlets hailed him as the 'Lion of the North' foretold in prophecy and a new Gideon. Yet confessional rhetoric coexisted with alliances across confessional lines, notably Catholic France's subsidies to Lutheran Sweden.
religiousCauses: The Peace of Augsburg (1555) excluded Calvinists and left disputes over secularised church lands, which generated decades of legal and political conflict.
Habsburg rulers, especially Ferdinand II, believed they had a religious duty to restore Catholicism in their lands, threatening Protestant liberties in Bohemia and Austria.
Bohemian Protestants saw the violation of the Letter of Majesty (1609) as an attack on their faith and rights.
The Edict of Restitution (1629) turned a dynastic war into a struggle for the survival of Protestantism in large parts of Germany.
Militant Calvinist networks, centred on the Palatinate, interpreted the conflict in apocalyptic terms as a decisive battle against the papacy.
otherCauses: The constitutional balance of the Holy Roman Empire between emperor and princes was contested, and many princes feared imperial absolutism.
Rivalry between the Habsburgs and France, and the Spanish need to keep the 'Spanish Road' to the Netherlands open, internationalised the conflict.
Swedish and Danish ambitions in the Baltic and northern Germany drove their interventions as much as Protestant solidarity.
Mercenary armies financed by plunder and contributions sustained the fighting, giving commanders such as Wallenstein their own interests in continuing it.
Economic strain, currency debasement (the Kipper- und Wipperzeit of 1619–23) and climate-driven harvest failures deepened social distress.
triggers: Ferdinand of Styria's election as king of Bohemia in 1617 and restrictions on Protestant church building at Broumov and Hrob.
The Defenestration of Prague on 23 May 1618.
The Bohemian estates' offer of the crown to the Calvinist Frederick V in August 1619.

timeline.text: Rudolf II grants the Bohemian Letter of Majesty; the Catholic League forms in answer to the Protestant Union.
Defenestration of Prague; the Bohemian revolt begins.
Ferdinand II is elected emperor; the Bohemians elect Frederick V king.
Battle of the White Mountain; Frederick, the 'Winter King', flees.
Execution of 27 Bohemian leaders in Prague; re-Catholicisation begins.
Christian IV of Denmark is defeated at Lutter.
Edict of Restitution; Peace of Lübeck takes Denmark out of the war.
Gustavus Adolphus lands in Pomerania.
Sack of Magdeburg (May); Swedish victory at Breitenfeld (September).
Gustavus Adolphus is killed at Lützen.
Wallenstein is assassinated; imperial and Spanish victory at Nördlingen.
Peace of Prague; France declares war on Spain.
French victory over Spain at Rocroi; congresses gather at Münster and Osnabrück.
Peace of Westphalia signed on 24 October.

keyPeople.name: Ferdinand II
keyPeople.focus: Crushed the Bohemian revolt, re-Catholicised Bohemia and Austria and issued the Edict of Restitution, which he regarded as a matter of conscience.
keyPeople.outcome: Forced to suspend the Edict in the Peace of Prague (1635); died before the war's end.

keyPeople.name: Frederick V of the Palatinate
keyPeople.role: Elector Palatine and king of Bohemia (1619–1620)
keyPeople.focus: Accepted the Bohemian crown as leader of the Calvinist cause and was routed at the White Mountain.
keyPeople.outcome: Lost both Bohemia and his electorate and died in exile; mocked as the 'Winter King'.

keyPeople.name: Johann Tserclaes, Count of Tilly
keyPeople.role: Commander of the Catholic League army
keyPeople.focus: A devout Catholic soldier trained by the Jesuits, he won at the White Mountain and Lutter and commanded the army that sacked Magdeburg.
keyPeople.outcome: Defeated at Breitenfeld and mortally wounded at the Lech in 1632; his responsibility for Magdeburg is still debated.

keyPeople.name: Albrecht von Wallenstein
keyPeople.focus: A Bohemian convert to Catholicism who raised and financed huge imperial armies by contributions, he fought for power and reward more than for faith.
keyPeople.outcome: Dismissed in 1630, recalled after Breitenfeld, and murdered at Eger in 1634 on suspicion of treason.

keyPeople.name: Gustavus Adolphus
keyPeople.focus: Intervened in 1630 as protector of German Protestantism and of Swedish interests, winning at Breitenfeld and Lützen.
keyPeople.outcome: Killed at Lützen; honoured as a Protestant hero, and the Gustav-Adolf-Werk relief society for diaspora Protestants bears his name.

keyPeople.name: Maximilian I of Bavaria
keyPeople.role: Duke, later Elector, of Bavaria and head of the Catholic League
keyPeople.focus: Financed and directed the League army and received the Palatine electoral title as reward.
keyPeople.outcome: Kept the Upper Palatinate and the electoral dignity at Westphalia.

keyPeople.name: Cardinal Richelieu
keyPeople.focus: Subsidised Protestant Sweden and finally brought Catholic France into the war against the Habsburgs, placing reason of state above confessional solidarity.
keyPeople.outcome: Died in 1642; his policy was continued by Mazarin and rewarded at Westphalia.

keyPeople.name: Wilhelm Lamormaini
keyPeople.focus: Urged the emperor to issue and uphold the Edict of Restitution as a religious obligation.
keyPeople.outcome: His influence declined after the Peace of Prague, which he opposed.

keyPeople.name: Jan Amos Comenius
keyPeople.role: Bishop of the Unity of Brethren and educator
keyPeople.focus: Lost his family and home in the war and went into lifelong exile after the re-Catholicisation of Bohemia.
keyPeople.outcome: Became a celebrated educational reformer and advocate of universal peace; died in Amsterdam.

keyPeople.name: Axel Oxenstierna
keyPeople.focus: Directed Swedish policy and the Heilbronn League after Gustavus's death and kept Sweden in the war until favourable terms were secured.
keyPeople.outcome: Secured Western Pomerania and Bremen-Verden for Sweden at Westphalia.

casualties.note: Peter H. Wilson estimates that the population of the Empire fell by around 5 million, perhaps 20 per cent, between 1618 and 1648, from a pre-war population of roughly 20 million; older estimates such as Günther Franz's suggested losses of a third or more. Most deaths were caused by epidemic disease, famine and displacement rather than battle, and losses varied greatly by region. Figures are reconstructions from parish registers, tax records and later censuses and remain uncertain.

effects: The Peace of Westphalia created a durable legal settlement for three confessions in the Empire and limited the power of rulers to change their subjects' religion.
The Habsburgs' attempt to build a strong Catholic imperial monarchy failed, and the princes' 'German liberty' was confirmed.
Sweden and France emerged as great powers, and Dutch and Swiss independence was recognised.
Central Europe suffered demographic and economic devastation from which some regions took generations to recover.
Bohemia and Austria were transformed into overwhelmingly Catholic lands, with a lasting baroque Catholic culture.
effectsOnChurch: Bohemian Protestantism, including the Unity of Brethren, was almost destroyed at home and survived chiefly in exile and in hidden communities that later fed the Moravian renewal at Herrnhut.
Calvinism gained legal recognition in the Empire, and confessional borders were essentially frozen around the 1624 normative year.
Innocent X's protest against the peace was ignored, showing the papacy's diminished role in European diplomacy.
Revulsion at confessional warfare encouraged irenic theology, Pietism's emphasis on inward faith and, later, Enlightenment arguments for toleration.
Lutheran devotional literature and hymnody of the period, such as the hymns of Paul Gerhardt, bore deep marks of suffering and consolation.
conflicts.legacy: For centuries German memory treated the Thirty Years' War as the greatest catastrophe before the twentieth century, captured in Grimmelshausen's Simplicissimus and the prints of Jacques Callot's Miseries of War. Westphalia became a symbol of the sovereign state system and of the political settlement of religious conflict. Recent historians question whether the war was really a 'war of religion', but agree that it discredited the idea of restoring Christian unity by force and changed how Europeans thought about the relationship between faith and state power.

dissenters.name: Hugo Grotius
dissenters.text: The Dutch jurist wrote in De iure belli ac pacis (1625) that he had seen throughout the Christian world a licence in making war of which even barbarous nations would be ashamed, and sought to bind Christians to legal limits on the causes and conduct of war.

dissenters.name: Jan Amos Comenius
dissenters.text: The exiled Brethren bishop called for reconciliation among Christians and nations, appealing for a general reform of human affairs and later addressing his Angelus Pacis (1667) to European peace negotiators.

dissenters.name: Georg Calixtus
dissenters.text: The Helmstedt Lutheran theologian argued that Lutherans, Reformed and Catholics shared the faith of the first five centuries and should seek reconciliation rather than condemnation; he took part in the irenic Colloquy of Thorn in 1645.

dissenters.name: Andreas Gryphius
dissenters.text: The Lutheran poet's sonnet 'Tränen des Vaterlandes' (1636) mourned burned churches, slaughtered citizens and souls lost amid the war, a lament for what Christians were doing to one another.

campaigns.title: The march of Gustavus Adolphus
campaigns.people: Gustavus Adolphus and the Swedish army
campaigns.text: Landing in Pomerania in July 1630, Gustavus secured the Oder, defeated Tilly at Breitenfeld, wintered in the Catholic Rhineland, forced the Lech crossing where Tilly was mortally wounded and occupied Munich. After a stand-off with Wallenstein at Nuremberg he marched into Saxony and was killed at Lützen.

campaigns.title: The Catholic League's march on Prague
campaigns.people: Maximilian of Bavaria, Tilly and the imperial commander Bucquoy
campaigns.text: After subduing Upper Austria, the League and imperial armies advanced into southern Bohemia, took Písek, shadowed the Bohemian army towards Rakovník and caught it on the White Mountain outside Prague on 8 November 1620.

conflicts.name: The Wars of the Three Kingdoms, the English Civil War and Cromwell in Ireland
conflicts.religionRoleNote: John Morrill famously argued that the English Civil War was 'not the first European revolution' but 'the last of the Wars of Religion': many who took up arms did so because they feared popery and Laudian 'innovation' or, on the other side, the destruction of the Church of England. Conrad Russell explained the breakdown through three interacting problems: religious division between and within the kingdoms, the strains of ruling multiple kingdoms, and royal financial weakness. Marxist historians such as Christopher Hill emphasised social and economic change, while others stress constitutional conflict over taxation and parliamentary rights. In Scotland the Covenant made religion the explicit cause; in Ireland confessional identity was bound up with land, colonisation and ethnicity. Religion was therefore a major cause, not the only one, and its weight varied between the three kingdoms.

sides.name: Royalists
sides.faith: Episcopalian Church of England, with many Catholic supporters
leaders: William Cavendish, Earl (later Marquess) of Newcastle
James Butler, Earl (later Marquess) of Ormond

sides.name: English Parliamentarians and the New Model Army
Confederate Catholics of Ireland
sides.faith: Roman Catholic (Gaelic Irish and Old English)

conflicts.summary: A linked series of wars in Scotland, Ireland, England and Wales that began with Scottish resistance to Charles I's religious policies, included the Irish Catholic rising of 1641, the English Civil Wars, the execution of the king and the Cromwellian conquest of Ireland and Scotland. Preachers on every side cast the struggle as God's cause; the massacres of Protestant settlers in 1641 and of the garrisons and townspeople of Drogheda and Wexford in 1649 left lasting sectarian memories.
conflicts.story:
Charles I ruled three kingdoms with three different religious settlements: an episcopal Church of England, a Church of Scotland with a strong Presbyterian tradition, and an Ireland whose majority remained Catholic under a Protestant established church and an expanding Protestant plantation. Under Archbishop William Laud the king promoted ceremonial worship, the 'beauty of holiness' and anti-Calvinist clergy, which Puritans regarded as a creeping return to popery. When a new Prayer Book was imposed on Scotland without consulting its General Assembly, its first reading in St Giles' Cathedral, Edinburgh, on 23 July 1637 provoked a riot. In February 1638 Scots of all ranks signed the National Covenant, pledging to defend the reformed religion, and in November the Glasgow Assembly abolished episcopacy.

Charles's attempts to coerce the Scots in the Bishops' Wars of 1639 and 1640 failed; a Scottish army defeated royal forces at Newburn and occupied Newcastle, forcing the king to summon what became the Long Parliament. Parliament impeached Laud and executed the king's Irish deputy, the Earl of Strafford, in 1641. In October 1641 Catholic Irish gentry in Ulster rose, fearing a militant Puritan Parliament and seeking to reverse plantation. The rising quickly became a popular attack on Protestant settlers: thousands were killed, including about a hundred men, women and children drowned at Portadown bridge, and many more died of exposure after being stripped and driven from their homes. Inflated reports in England spoke of 100,000 or more Protestants massacred; modern historians, working from the 1641 depositions, estimate several thousand killed directly. These reports convinced many English Protestants that a popish plot threatened them all.

Distrust over who should command an army to suppress the Irish rising brought matters to a head. After the king's failed attempt to arrest five members of the Commons in January 1642, both sides raised forces, and Charles raised his standard at Nottingham in August 1642. The indecisive battle of Edgehill (October 1642) opened a war that divided counties, towns and families. In 1643 Parliament allied with the Scots in the Solemn League and Covenant, promising to reform religion in England and Ireland 'according to the word of God and the example of the best reformed churches', and summoned the Westminster Assembly of divines. Meanwhile the Irish Catholic leaders formed the Confederation of Kilkenny, whose oath pledged loyalty to the king and the free exercise of the Catholic religion.

The combined armies of Parliament and the Scots won at Marston Moor in July 1644. The reorganised New Model Army under Fairfax, with Cromwell commanding the cavalry, destroyed the king's main army at Naseby in June 1645; after the battle Parliamentarian soldiers killed or mutilated women in the Royalist baggage train, some of them believed to be Irish. In Scotland the Marquess of Montrose won a series of victories for the king with Irish and Highland troops in 1644–45, including the sack of Aberdeen, before his defeat at Philiphaugh, after which Covenanter troops massacred Irish prisoners and camp followers. Laud was beheaded in January 1645. In Ireland the papal nuncio Rinuccini pressed the Confederates to secure full Catholic establishment, and Owen Roe O'Neill defeated a Scottish army at Benburb in 1646, but quarrels over terms with the king divided the Confederation.

Charles surrendered to the Scots in 1646 and was handed to Parliament, but his negotiations with the Scots provoked a Second Civil War in 1648, which Cromwell ended at Preston. Convinced that the king was a 'man of blood' who had defied God's verdict in battle, the army purged Parliament in December 1648, and Charles I was tried and beheaded outside the Banqueting House in Whitehall on 30 January 1649. England became a republic, and the Church of England's bishops and Prayer Book had already been abolished.

In August 1649 Cromwell landed at Dublin. On 11 September his troops stormed Drogheda and, on his orders, killed the garrison of some 2,500–3,000 men together with Catholic clergy and an unknown number of civilians; Cromwell called it 'a righteous judgement of God upon these barbarous wretches' who had shed so much innocent blood in 1641. At Wexford in October soldiers ran out of control during negotiations and killed some 2,000 defenders and townspeople. Cromwell left Ireland in May 1650 after taking Clonmel at heavy cost, and his successors completed the conquest by 1653 amid famine, plague and guerrilla war. In Scotland, which had proclaimed Charles II king, Cromwell defeated the Covenanters at Dunbar in September 1650, after which thousands of prisoners died on a forced march and in captivity at Durham; Charles II's invasion of England ended at Worcester in September 1651.

The Cromwellian settlement confiscated most remaining Catholic-owned land in Ireland, transplanted many landowners west of the Shannon to Connacht and Clare, banished priests and sent thousands of Irish to the West Indies as bound labourers. The share of Irish land in Catholic hands fell from about three-fifths in 1641 to well under a quarter after the Restoration. Oliver Cromwell became Lord Protector in December 1653. Within England the wars had produced an explosion of religious sects, including Baptists, Fifth Monarchists and Quakers, but the monarchy and the episcopal Church of England were restored in 1660, and the Act of Uniformity of 1662 ejected nonconforming ministers.
conflicts.nameOfGod: Each side claimed God's favour. Royalists fought for 'God and the King' and the divine right of monarchs and defended the Church of England's bishops and Prayer Book. The Scots swore the National Covenant (1638) and, with Parliament, the Solemn League and Covenant (1643), binding nations to God by oath; Covenanter ministers preached that sparing enemies of the Lord was sin, and the cry 'Jesus and no quarter' was later associated with the massacre after Philiphaugh. Parliament held monthly fast days at which preachers such as Stephen Marshall, in his sermon 'Meroz Cursed' (1642), denounced neutrality as a curse from God. Cromwell read victories as 'providences' and 'dispensations' showing God's verdict, and the New Model Army marched singing psalms. The Irish Confederates' motto was 'Pro Deo, pro Rege, pro Patria Hibernia unanimis', and Rinuccini threatened excommunication against Catholics who accepted a truce with the Protestant royalists.
religiousCauses: Laudian ceremonialism and anti-Calvinist church policy convinced many English and Scottish Protestants that the king was leading the church back towards Rome.
The imposition of the Scottish Prayer Book in 1637 without the consent of the Kirk provoked the National Covenant and armed resistance.
Fear of a 'popish plot', intensified by Catholic influence at court around Queen Henrietta Maria and by reports from Ireland, shaped Parliamentary politics.
Irish Catholics sought freedom of worship and feared that a Puritan Parliament would suppress their religion completely.
Disagreement over whether to abolish episcopacy 'root and branch' split the English political nation in 1641–42.
otherCauses: Charles I's financial expedients during the Personal Rule (1629–40), such as Ship Money, raised constitutional objections to taxation without Parliament.
The 'problem of multiple kingdoms' meant that policies made in London provoked resistance in Edinburgh and Dublin.
Plantation and confiscation of Irish land since the sixteenth century created deep ethnic and economic grievance.
Charles I's political inflexibility and distrust of his opponents made compromise difficult.
Local and factional rivalries, and fears for property and order, influenced many people's choice of side.
triggers: The Prayer Book riot in St Giles' Cathedral, Edinburgh, on 23 July 1637.
The outbreak of the Irish rising on 23 October 1641.
Charles I's attempt to arrest the Five Members on 4 January 1642.
The raising of the royal standard at Nottingham on 22 August 1642.

timeline.text: Prayer Book riot at St Giles', Edinburgh.
National Covenant signed; the Glasgow Assembly abolishes episcopacy.
First Bishops' War.
Second Bishops' War; the Long Parliament meets.
Strafford executed; Irish rising and killings of Protestant settlers in Ulster; Grand Remonstrance.
Civil war begins in England; battle of Edgehill; Confederation of Kilkenny formed.
Solemn League and Covenant; Westminster Assembly meets.
Battle of Marston Moor; Montrose's campaign in Scotland begins.
Laud executed; New Model Army wins at Naseby; Montrose defeated at Philiphaugh.
Owen Roe O'Neill wins at Benburb; Charles I surrenders to the Scots.
Second Civil War; Pride's Purge of Parliament.
Execution of Charles I; Cromwell storms Drogheda and Wexford.
Charles II defeated at Worcester.
Last Irish forces surrender; Cromwell becomes Lord Protector.

keyPeople.name: Charles I
keyPeople.role: King of England, Scotland and Ireland
keyPeople.focus: Promoted Laudian church policy, attempted to impose it on Scotland and led the Royalist cause in the Civil War.
keyPeople.outcome: Tried and executed in 1649; venerated by some Anglicans as 'King Charles the Martyr'.

keyPeople.name: William Laud
keyPeople.focus: Enforced ceremonial uniformity and the 'beauty of holiness', prosecuted Puritan critics and supported the Scottish Prayer Book.
keyPeople.outcome: Impeached by the Long Parliament and beheaded on Tower Hill in 1645.

keyPeople.name: Oliver Cromwell
keyPeople.focus: A convinced Independent Puritan, he led cavalry at Marston Moor and Naseby, signed the king's death warrant and conducted the conquest of Ireland in 1649–50.
keyPeople.outcome: Ruled as Lord Protector from 1653 and allowed wide toleration to Protestant sects and, unofficially, readmitted Jews; reviled in Ireland for Drogheda and Wexford.

keyPeople.name: Sir Thomas Fairfax
keyPeople.role: Commander-in-chief of the New Model Army
keyPeople.focus: Won Naseby and ended the First Civil War; enforced the army's political demands in 1647–48.
keyPeople.outcome: Withdrew from the king's trial and later helped bring about the Restoration.

keyPeople.name: Archibald Campbell, Marquess of Argyll
keyPeople.focus: Directed Covenanter policy and the alliance with the English Parliament, and later crowned Charles II at Scone in 1651.
keyPeople.outcome: Executed for treason after the Restoration in 1661.

keyPeople.name: James Graham, Marquess of Montrose
keyPeople.focus: An early signatory of the Covenant who changed sides, he won six victories for the king in 1644–45 with Irish and Highland troops.
keyPeople.outcome: Defeated at Philiphaugh; captured on a later expedition and hanged in Edinburgh in 1650.

keyPeople.name: Owen Roe O'Neill
keyPeople.role: General of the Confederate Ulster army
keyPeople.focus: A veteran of Spanish service who fought for Catholic rights and Irish land, he won the battle of Benburb in 1646 and backed the nuncio's hard line.
keyPeople.outcome: Died in November 1649 as Cromwell's campaign advanced.

keyPeople.name: Giovanni Battista Rinuccini
keyPeople.role: Papal nuncio to the Irish Confederation
keyPeople.focus: Insisted on full public establishment of Catholicism and excommunicated supporters of the 1648 truce with the royalist Inchiquin, splitting the Confederates.
keyPeople.outcome: Left Ireland in 1649; his mission is still debated as principled or disastrous.

keyPeople.name: James Butler, Earl of Ormond
keyPeople.origin: London, of an Old English Irish family
keyPeople.focus: A Protestant who negotiated peace treaties with the Catholic Confederates in 1646 and 1649 to unite Irish forces for the king.
keyPeople.outcome: Left Ireland in 1650; returned as Lord Lieutenant after the Restoration.

keyPeople.name: John Pym
keyPeople.focus: Led the Commons against the king, warned of a popish plot and negotiated the Solemn League and Covenant with the Scots.
keyPeople.outcome: Died of illness in December 1643.

casualties.note: Charles Carlton estimated about 190,000 deaths in England and Wales from fighting and war-related disease (some 3.7 per cent of the population) and about 60,000 in Scotland. Losses in Ireland, from fighting, massacre, famine and plague, were proportionally far higher: Sir William Petty's contemporary figure of over 600,000 is now considered too high, but modern historians such as Pádraig Lenihan still suggest the loss of perhaps 15–20 per cent of the population, roughly 200,000 or more. All figures are reconstructions with wide margins of error.

effects: Charles I was executed and England, Scotland and Ireland were united for the first time under a single republican government.
The Cromwellian conquest and land settlement transferred most Irish land to Protestant owners and laid foundations of the Protestant Ascendancy.
The monarchy and House of Lords were abolished and then restored in 1660, but the relationship between Crown and Parliament was permanently changed.
Ireland and Scotland suffered military occupation, and Ireland endured famine, plague and population loss.
Political ideas of popular sovereignty, religious liberty and the rights of 'freeborn Englishmen' emerged from Leveller and army debates.
effectsOnChurch: Episcopacy and the Book of Common Prayer were abolished in England during the 1640s and restored, with the ejection of some 2,000 Puritan ministers, after 1660–62.
The Westminster Assembly produced the Westminster Confession, catechisms and Directory for Public Worship, which became the standards of Presbyterian churches worldwide.
Independent, Baptist and Quaker movements grew rapidly amid wartime freedom, creating a permanent English Nonconformity.
Irish Catholicism was driven underground, its clergy banished or killed, and Catholic identity in Ireland was fused with memory of dispossession.
Memories of 1641 and of Drogheda shaped Protestant and Catholic sectarian narratives in Ireland for centuries.
conflicts.legacy: The wars remain contested ground. In England they are remembered as a struggle over Parliament and liberty; in Scotland through the Covenanting tradition; in Ireland through the twin memories of 1641 and Cromwell's 'curse'. Historians now read them as a 'British' crisis in which the religious divisions of three kingdoms collided, and the experience of godly warfare and its failure fed later arguments for religious toleration.

dissenters.name: George Fox
dissenters.text: Imprisoned at Derby in 1651, the Quaker founder refused an offer of a captaincy in the Commonwealth army, saying that he lived 'in the virtue of that life and power that took away the occasion of all wars'; the Quakers' 1661 declaration to Charles II made pacifism a mark of the movement.

dissenters.name: Lucius Cary, Viscount Falkland
dissenters.text: A moderate royalist and friend of Christian humanists who longed for compromise, he was remembered by Clarendon as repeating 'Peace, peace' in his despair at the war before he was killed at Newbury in 1643.

dissenters.name: Gerrard Winstanley
dissenters.text: The Digger leader rejected the use of the sword to establish God's kingdom, calling instead for the peaceful common cultivation of the land in 1649–50.

dissenters.name: Richard Baxter
dissenters.text: A Parliamentarian army chaplain who opposed the regicide and the army's later political actions; he later wrote of the bitter fruits of the war and worked for reconciliation among Protestants.

theatres.name: St Giles' Cathedral Prayer Book riot
Battle of Philiphaugh and massacre of prisoners

campaigns.title: Cromwell's Irish campaign
campaigns.people: Oliver Cromwell and the New Model Army
campaigns.text: Cromwell sailed from Milford Haven to Dublin in August 1649, stormed Drogheda and Wexford, took New Ross, failed before Waterford in winter, then captured Kilkenny and, at heavy cost, Clonmel before sailing home from Youghal in May 1650.

campaigns.title: Montrose's year of victories
campaigns.people: James Graham, Marquess of Montrose, and Alasdair Mac Colla
campaigns.text: With Irish Confederate troops under Alasdair Mac Colla and Highland clansmen, Montrose won at Tippermuir, sacked Aberdeen, crushed the Campbells at Inverlochy and won at Auldearn, Alford and Kilsyth before being surprised and defeated at Philiphaugh in September 1645.

conflicts.name: The Shimabara Rebellion of Japanese Christians
conflicts.region: Shimabara Peninsula and Amakusa Islands, Kyushu, Japan
conflicts.religionRoleNote: The Tokugawa regime presented the rising as a Christian rebellion, and it used Christian banners, slogans and a messianic youth leader in regions that had been heavily Catholic before the ban of 1614. Many earlier historians, however, treated it chiefly as a peasant revolt against crushing taxation, famine and brutal collection by the daimyo Matsukura Katsuie and Terazawa Katataka, joined by masterless samurai of the former Christian lords Arima and Konishi. Recent Japanese scholarship (for example Kanda Chisato and Ōhashi Yukihiro) has re-emphasised its religious, millenarian character: many former apostates publicly returned to Christianity, non-Christian villagers were pressed to convert, and temples and shrines were burned. Most historians now see an inseparable fusion of economic desperation and Christian hope.

sides.name: Shimabara and Amakusa insurgents
sides.faith: Kirishitan (Japanese Catholic, many returned apostates), with non-Christian peasants

sides.name: Tokugawa shogunate and the Kyushu daimyo
Dutch East India Company (in support of the shogunate)

conflicts.summary: A rising of peasants, fishermen and masterless samurai in the formerly Christian districts of Shimabara and Amakusa in western Kyushu, led in name by the teenage Amakusa Shirō and fought under Catholic banners. After defeating the first assaults, some 27,000 or more rebels, including women and children, were besieged in the ruined Hara Castle and killed almost to the last person in April 1638. The rebellion confirmed the shogunate's resolve to eradicate Christianity and close Japan to the Portuguese.
conflicts.story:
Catholicism had spread rapidly in Kyushu after Francis Xavier's arrival in 1549. The Shimabara peninsula was ruled by the Christian daimyo Arima Harunobu and the Amakusa islands by the Christian general Konishi Yukinaga, and by 1600 their lands were among the most Christian regions of Asia. After Konishi's execution in 1600 and Arima's fall in 1612, new lords took over: the Matsukura family in Shimabara and the Terazawa in Amakusa. The Tokugawa ban on Christianity in 1614 expelled missionaries and began decades of persecution: the 'Great Martyrdom' of Nagasaki in 1622, the use of fumie (images to be trampled) and, around Shimabara, the torture of Christians in the boiling springs of Mount Unzen under Matsukura Shigemasa from 1627.

Matsukura Katsuie, who inherited Shimabara in 1630, imposed taxes far beyond the domain's real yield to pay for castle building and service to the shogun. Peasants who failed to pay were tortured, and accounts tell of men dressed in straw raincoats set alight (the 'mino odori', straw-coat dance) and of family members held hostage. Several years of poor harvests and famine in the mid-1630s pushed villages beyond endurance. At the same time rumours spread of a prophecy attributed to a missionary expelled a quarter of a century earlier, that a heavenly youth would appear amid portents to save the Christians. Many villagers identified this figure with Masuda Shirō, the sixteen-year-old son of a former Konishi retainer, credited with miracles.

In December 1637 (the tenth month of Kan'ei 14) villagers in Arima killed a local official who had broken up a Christian gathering and destroyed a sacred image. The rising spread rapidly through southern Shimabara: rebels killed officials and Buddhist priests, burned temples and shrines and besieged Shimabara Castle without success. Across the water, Amakusa villagers rose, defeated Terazawa troops and besieged Tomioka Castle, again without taking it. Early in 1638 the insurgents of both regions gathered in Hara Castle, an abandoned Arima fortress on cliffs overlooking the Ariake Sea, which they repaired and fortified. Estimates of the number inside range from about 27,000 to 37,000 men, women and children.

The shogunate sent Itakura Shigemasa to command the Kyushu domains. His assaults failed, and in a final attack on the first day of the new year (February 1638) he was killed with thousands of his men. Matsudaira Nobutsuna, a senior councillor, then took command of an army that grew to over 120,000. He ordered a blockade, siege works and mining, and asked the Dutch at Hirado for help: the ship de Ryp under Nicolaes Couckebacker bombarded the castle for about two weeks, firing several hundred rounds. The Dutch participation, Protestant Europeans firing on Japanese Catholics, was remembered with bitterness by Catholic writers and with some embarrassment by the Dutch themselves.

By April the defenders were starving; captured rebels were found with only seaweed and leaves in their stomachs. On 12 April 1638 (the 28th day of the second month) the shogunal army stormed the castle. The defenders resisted for two days, and virtually all were then killed, including women and children; the buildings were burned and the castle later demolished. Amakusa Shirō's head was displayed in Nagasaki. The painter Yamada Emosaku, who had secretly corresponded with the besiegers, was reportedly the only notable survivor.

The aftermath was severe. Matsukura Katsuie was condemned and beheaded in 1638, the only daimyo executed in this way in the Edo period, and Terazawa lost Amakusa. The shogunate concluded that Portuguese missionaries and traders were a permanent danger: in 1639 it expelled the Portuguese, and in 1641 the Dutch were confined to the artificial island of Dejima in Nagasaki harbour. The depopulated peninsula was resettled with migrants from other regions. Every household was required to register with a Buddhist temple and certify annually that it was not Christian, informers were rewarded, and the 'closed country' policy remained in force until the 1850s.

Christianity survived only in secret among the Kakure Kirishitan of the Nagasaki and Gotō regions, who passed on prayers and rites without priests for over two centuries. In modern Japan Amakusa Shirō became a romantic, sometimes nationalist, hero of resistance. The Catholic Church has not counted the dead of Hara Castle among the beatified martyrs of Japan, because they took up arms, though many Japanese Catholics remember them with sympathy.
conflicts.nameOfGod: The rebels marched under Christian banners and cried 'Jesus', 'Maria' and 'Santiago'. A surviving banner, attributed to Amakusa Shirō and now in the Amakusa Christian Museum, shows two angels adoring a chalice and host beneath the Portuguese inscription 'Louvado seja o Santíssimo Sacramento' ('Praised be the Most Holy Sacrament'). Shirō was revered as the heaven-sent youth of prophecy, and rebel letters thrown into the besiegers' camp declared that they fought for their faith and that the next world mattered more than this one. Apostates were urged to return to the faith and non-Christians were pressed to convert. The shogunate in turn condemned Christianity as an 'evil teaching' (jakyō) that made subjects disloyal, and used the rebellion to justify the systematic eradication of the faith.
religiousCauses: The 1614 ban and the persecution of Christians, including torture at the Unzen hot springs, fell especially hard on the formerly Christian domains of Shimabara and Amakusa.
Many who had apostatised under pressure publicly returned to Christianity, and the rising became a collective act of repentance and faith.
A prophecy of a heaven-sent youth who would save the Christians focused hopes on Amakusa Shirō and gave the revolt a millenarian character.
Without priests since 1614, lay confraternities had maintained Christian networks that could quickly mobilise villages.
otherCauses: Matsukura Katsuie and Terazawa Katataka imposed taxes far beyond what their lands could bear and enforced them with torture.
Famine and crop failures in the mid-1630s left many villages starving.
Masterless samurai of the dispossessed Arima and Konishi houses provided military leadership and resented the new lords.
Local grievances against officials and the strains of the new Tokugawa order on peripheral Kyushu communities.
triggers: The killing of a local official in Arima village in December 1637 after he broke up a Christian assembly and destroyed a sacred image.
Rumours that the heaven-sent youth had appeared in the person of Amakusa Shirō.
The rising of the Amakusa villagers against the Terazawa administration days later, which turned a local revolt into a regional war.

timeline.text: Francis Xavier arrives in Kagoshima; Catholicism later spreads widely in Kyushu.
Execution of the Christian daimyo Konishi Yukinaga; Amakusa passes to the Terazawa.
The Tokugawa shogunate bans Christianity and expels missionaries.
Great Martyrdom of Nagasaki: 55 Christians executed.
Torture of Christians at the Unzen hot springs begins under Matsukura Shigemasa.
Rising breaks out in Shimabara and Amakusa; sieges of Shimabara and Tomioka castles fail.
Rebels occupy Hara Castle; Itakura Shigemasa is killed; Dutch bombardment; Hara falls on 12 April and the defenders are massacred.
Matsukura Katsuie is executed for misgovernment.
The Portuguese are expelled from Japan.
The Dutch are confined to Dejima; temple registration is tightened.
Edicts against Christianity are finally removed.

keyPeople.name: Amakusa Shirō Tokisada (Masuda Shirō)
keyPeople.role: Charismatic youth leader of the rebellion
keyPeople.focus: Baptised as Jerónimo, he was hailed as the prophesied heavenly youth and became the symbolic head of the rising, while experienced rōnin directed its military operations.
keyPeople.outcome: Killed when Hara Castle fell; his head was displayed at Nagasaki. He became a legendary figure in Japanese culture.

keyPeople.name: Matsukura Katsuie
keyPeople.focus: His crushing taxes and cruel enforcement, together with persecution of Christians, provoked the revolt.
keyPeople.outcome: Condemned by the shogunate and beheaded in 1638.

keyPeople.name: Itakura Shigemasa
keyPeople.role: First shogunal commander against the rebels
keyPeople.focus: Led the early assaults on Hara Castle, which failed with heavy losses.
keyPeople.outcome: Killed in the attack of February 1638.

keyPeople.name: Matsudaira Nobutsuna
keyPeople.role: Senior councillor (rōjū) and commander of the siege
keyPeople.focus: Replaced frontal assault with blockade, siege works and Dutch naval bombardment, and directed the final storming of Hara Castle.
keyPeople.outcome: Remained one of the most powerful officials of the shogunate.

keyPeople.name: Tokugawa Iemitsu
keyPeople.focus: Ordered the suppression of the rising and drew from it the lesson that Christianity must be eradicated.
keyPeople.outcome: Completed the exclusion of the Portuguese and the 'closed country' system.

keyPeople.name: Yamada Emosaku
keyPeople.focus: A Christian painter who served the rebels, he secretly offered to betray the castle to the besiegers.
keyPeople.outcome: Reportedly the only notable survivor; he later lived in Edo, and religious paintings are attributed to him.

keyPeople.name: Nicolaes Couckebacker
keyPeople.role: Head of the Dutch East India Company factory at Hirado
keyPeople.focus: At the shogunate's request he sent the ship de Ryp to bombard Hara Castle.
keyPeople.outcome: The Dutch assistance helped secure their position as the only Europeans allowed to trade with Japan.

casualties.note: Most deaths were among the defenders of Hara Castle, whom contemporary and modern estimates put at about 27,000 to 37,000, including many women and children; almost all were killed in or after the final assault. Shogunal losses in killed and wounded were also heavy, reported in Japanese records as several thousand to over 10,000 casualties, but the proportion killed is uncertain.

effects: The shogunate expelled the Portuguese in 1639 and confined the Dutch to Dejima in 1641, completing Japan's policy of restricted foreign contact.
Temple registration and annual certification that households were not Christian became universal, binding every Japanese family to a Buddhist temple.
The Shimabara peninsula, largely depopulated, was resettled with migrants from other regions.
The rebellion reinforced the shogunate's view of Christianity as a subversive foreign creed for more than two centuries.
effectsOnChurch: Open Christianity in Japan was destroyed, and the faith survived only among hidden Christians (Kakure Kirishitan) without priests until the 1860s.
Rewards for denouncing Christians and the systematic use of fumie made secret Christian life extremely dangerous.
The Catholic Church did not include the rebels among Japan's beatified martyrs, distinguishing armed resistance from martyrdom.
In Europe, Catholic writers cited the Dutch bombardment as evidence of Protestant complicity in persecution.
conflicts.legacy: The Shimabara Rebellion closed the 'Christian century' in Japan. For the Tokugawa it justified a policy of eradication and isolation; for Japanese Christians it became a painful memory of faith, desperation and slaughter. Novels, films and popular culture have made Amakusa Shirō an emblem of doomed rebellion, while historians continue to debate how far the revolt was a peasant uprising and how far a Christian holy war.

dissenters.name: The Kirishitan martyr tradition
dissenters.text: Japanese Catholic teaching under persecution, spread through lay confraternities and the martyrdom manuals of the Jesuits, urged believers to endure suffering and die for the faith rather than take up arms; many Christian communities, including those around Nagasaki, did not join the rising.

dissenters.name: Yamada Emosaku
dissenters.text: Whether from conviction or self-preservation, the rebel painter urged negotiation and secretly sought terms with the besiegers, later claiming that he had opposed the course of the rising.

theatres.name: Arima and Kuchinotsu, outbreak of the rising
Siege and massacre of Hara Castle

campaigns.title: The Amakusa insurgents' march to Hara
campaigns.people: Amakusa villagers and rōnin under Amakusa Shirō
campaigns.text: After defeating Terazawa forces near Hondo and failing to take Tomioka Castle, the Amakusa rebels crossed the strait to the Shimabara peninsula and joined the Shimabara insurgents in the ruined Hara Castle.

campaigns.title: Matsudaira Nobutsuna's march from Edo
campaigns.text: Sent from Edo to take over the campaign, Nobutsuna travelled west to Kyushu and arrived at Hara as Itakura's assaults failed, taking command of an army drawn from the Kyushu domains.

conflicts.name: The Camisard War of the Cévennes Huguenots
conflicts.religionRoleNote: The Camisards rose to restore the Reformed worship outlawed by the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes (1685), were led and directed by 'inspired' prophets, and targeted priests, churches and Catholic symbols; religion was both the stated and the real cause. Historians such as Philippe Joutard and W. Gregory Monahan have also shown the role of rural poverty, war taxation (the capitation of 1695) and regional resentment of royal intendants, and Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie placed the revolt within the long history of Languedoc peasant unrest. These factors shaped who joined and when, but the movement's identity, aims and language were overwhelmingly religious.

sides.name: Camisards ('Children of God')
sides.faith: Reformed Protestant (Huguenot), with a strong prophetic movement

sides.name: Royal government of Louis XIV and Catholic militias
leaders: Nicolas de Lamoignon de Basville, intendant of Languedoc

conflicts.summary: A guerrilla rising of Protestant peasants and artisans in the mountains of the Cévennes against Louis XIV's suppression of Protestantism. Led by young lay preachers and prophets who spoke in states of ecstatic inspiration, the Camisards fought royal armies to a standstill in 1702–04, burning churches and killing priests, while the crown responded with executions, massacres and the systematic burning of upland villages. The main revolt ended in 1704–05, with sporadic resistance until 1710.
conflicts.story:
The Edict of Nantes (1598) had granted French Protestants limited toleration, but Louis XIV progressively restricted it, sent dragoons to be billeted on Protestant households (the dragonnades of 1681–85) and finally revoked it by the Edict of Fontainebleau in October 1685. Protestant worship was forbidden, pastors were expelled on pain of death, while lay people were forbidden to emigrate and declared 'new converts' to Catholicism. Perhaps 150,000–200,000 Huguenots fled abroad nonetheless. In the Cévennes and Bas-Languedoc, where Protestants formed the majority in many communities, people continued to meet in secret assemblies in the 'Desert'. Lay preachers such as Claude Brousson, executed at Montpellier in 1698, kept the faith alive, and troops broke up assemblies, killing or sending participants to the galleys.

From the late 1680s a prophetic movement spread from the Dauphiné and the Vivarais into the Cévennes. Young men, women and even children fell into trances, trembled, and spoke in the language of Scripture, calling for repentance and announcing the fall of 'Babylon', meaning the Catholic Church. Pierre Jurieu, the exiled pastor in Rotterdam, had predicted from the book of Revelation that the restoration of French Protestantism would come in 1689. The authorities treated the prophets as dangerous fanatics, imprisoning and executing many of them.

On the night of 24 July 1702 a band of about fifty Protestants led by the prophet Esprit Séguier attacked the house of the abbé François de Langlade du Chaila, archpriest of the Cévennes and inspector of missions, at Le Pont-de-Montvert, where he held prisoners captured on their way to emigrate. They freed the prisoners and killed du Chaila, then killed several other priests and Catholic notables. Séguier was captured and burned alive at Le Pont-de-Montvert on 12 August 1702, but the revolt spread. Its fighters, called Camisards, perhaps from the white shirts (camisa in Occitan) worn on night raids, formed several bands under Rolland, Jean Cavalier, Abraham Mazel, Nicolas Jouany and others. At its height the movement may have had 2,000–3,000 fighters, supported by much of the Protestant population.

The Camisards fought a guerrilla war in the mountains and the plains around Alès, Anduze and Nîmes. They ambushed troops, burned churches and presbyteries, and killed priests and Catholic villagers, as in the attack on Fraissinet-de-Fourques in February 1703, which left around forty dead. Royal forces under Marshal Montrevel and the intendant Basville answered with summary executions, the breaking of rebels on the wheel and burnings. On 1 April 1703, Palm Sunday, Montrevel's troops surrounded a mill at the Agau gate of Nîmes where Protestants had gathered for worship, set it on fire and killed those who tried to escape. Catholic irregulars, known as the 'cadets of the Cross' or 'white Camisards', raided and massacred in Protestant villages.

From September to December 1703 the crown carried out the 'grand brûlement des Cévennes': the inhabitants of some 466 villages and hamlets in the upper Cévennes were ordered to leave, and their homes, crops and livestock were destroyed to deprive the rebels of support. In March 1704 Cavalier defeated royal troops at Martignargues, but his band was routed at Nages in April. The new commander, Marshal Villars, combined military pressure with offers of amnesty. In May 1704 Cavalier negotiated with Villars at Nîmes and agreed to surrender in return for a commission and permission for his men to leave France; his followers, who had fought for the restoration of their worship, regarded this as betrayal. Rolland was killed in August 1704 near the château of Castelnau, and his body was dragged through Nîmes and burned.

Most remaining leaders surrendered or were captured in 1704–05; a plot to renew the rising in 1705 ended with the execution of Ravanel and Catinat at Nîmes. Abraham Mazel, who escaped and returned, led a last attempt in the Vivarais in 1709 and was killed in 1710. In 1715 the young preacher Antoine Court held the first synod of the 'Church of the Desert', rejecting prophetic inspiration and armed resistance in favour of rebuilding a disciplined Reformed church under persecution. French Protestants gained civil status only with the Edict of Versailles in 1787 and full freedom of worship during the Revolution.

Several Camisard prophets, including Élie Marion, reached London in 1706, where the 'French Prophets' caused a sensation and won English followers; their ecstatic practice has been linked to later movements, including the Shakers. In France the Camisards became a symbol of Protestant memory and of resistance to tyranny. Since 1911 an annual assembly has gathered at the Mas Soubeyran in Mialet, Rolland's birthplace and now the Musée du Désert.
conflicts.nameOfGod: The Camisards called themselves the 'Children of God' and the 'troops of the Lord'. Their prophets, believed to be moved by the Holy Spirit, chose targets, judged traitors and ordered attacks, and the fighters went into battle singing Psalm 68 in Clément Marot's version, 'Que Dieu se montre seulement', known as the 'Psalm of battles'. They saw themselves as Israel fighting the idolaters and burned churches as houses of idolatry. Bishop Esprit Fléchier of Nîmes and royal officials condemned them as 'fanatics' and treated their inspiration as madness or imposture. Catholic militias wore crosses and called themselves the 'cadets of the Cross'; rumours that they acted under a papal bull of Clement XI granting indulgences circulated at the time, but no such bull has been found and the claim is generally doubted.
religiousCauses: The Revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685 outlawed Protestant worship and forced Huguenots to conform outwardly to Catholicism.
Forced attendance at Mass, the seizure of children for Catholic education and the punishment of secret assemblies created intense resentment.
A prophetic and apocalyptic movement convinced many that God was calling them to overthrow 'Babylon' and restore true worship.
The abbé du Chaila's mission work and imprisonment of would-be emigrants made him a symbol of religious coercion.
Executions of preachers such as Claude Brousson and of prophets fed a culture of martyrdom and resistance.
otherCauses: Heavy war taxation, including the capitation introduced in 1695 during Louis XIV's wars, burdened a poor mountain population.
The rugged terrain of the Cévennes favoured guerrilla warfare and made royal control difficult.
Regional resentment of the intendant Basville's authoritarian administration of Languedoc.
France's involvement in the War of the Spanish Succession tied down royal troops and encouraged hopes of help from Protestant England and the Dutch Republic.
triggers: The killing of the abbé du Chaila at Le Pont-de-Montvert on the night of 24 July 1702.
The execution of Esprit Séguier on 12 August 1702, which spread the revolt.
The intensification of military repression of secret assemblies and prophets in the Cévennes in the spring and summer of 1702.

timeline.text: Edict of Fontainebleau revokes the Edict of Nantes.
Prophetic movement spreads from the Dauphiné into the Vivarais and Cévennes.
The lay preacher Claude Brousson is executed at Montpellier.
Abbé du Chaila killed at Le Pont-de-Montvert (July); Esprit Séguier burned (August).
Massacre at the mill of the Agau, Nîmes (April); 'grand brûlement' of the upper Cévennes (September–December).
Cavalier victorious at Martignargues and defeated at Nages; he submits to Villars in May; Rolland killed in August.
Failed plot to renew the rising; Ravanel and Catinat executed at Nîmes.
